If EC holds, niche construction partly composes selection, so the two fail Woodward's independent-fixability condition and cannot stand in a causal relation. | [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) | Life as we know it | Friston (2013), J. R. Soc. Interface 10(86):20130475. Any ergodic random dynamical system whose states split into internal, sensory, active and external sets with a Markov blanket has internal and active states whose flow can be written as a gradient descent on a variational free energy of the blanket and internal states (Lemma 2.1, Eqs. 2.5–2.8). They therefore "appear" to do Bayesian inference about external states and to bound their own entropy. A simulated "primordial soup" of 128 coupled Lorenz subsystems forms a blanket-enclosed cluster whose internal states predict external motion (5 of 82 above a time-reversed null) and which disperses when blanket or internal states are lesioned. The paper says a candle flame cannot have a Markov blanket, and concedes that the universe holds countless blankets, conjecturing that minimum-entropy blankets mark life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md)), from the published text (the author's posted PDF of the journal version and the PMC full text). Worth reading as the founding statement of the Markov-blanket formulation of the free energy principle applied to life, and as the one text in the record that names a candle flame and says it is not lifelike. Read it as a redescription, not a derivation: its "heuristic proof" shows that the flow of an ergodic system with a Markov blanket can be written as a gradient flow on a variational free energy, by choosing the variational density to equal the posterior. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic; no heat or entropy production is computed. The simulation is one run, analysed with a blanket chosen by spectral clustering. |

Worth reading as the canonical statement of the "gradient-dissipation" view of life: living systems and ecosystems are dissipative structures that develop so as to degrade the solar gradient more completely, and the second law is "a necessary but not sufficient cause for life". Read the thermodynamics as a programme, not a derivation. The "restated second law" is offered as a corollary of Kestin's stability result but not derived from it. The ecological evidence is one stressed-versus-control marsh pair and a few thermal-scanner and satellite comparisons, all correlational. It draws no line between living and non-living dissipative structures beyond "memory" (DNA). |

The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the chapter list. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read. HAL now serves files behind an anti-bot challenge that requires a browser running JavaScript, and it states that the challenge is there against automated scrapers, so I did not try to get past it. A human reader can open the copy lawfully, and a reading from it would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-566.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Barandiaran, Di Paolo & Rohde (2009), Adaptive Behavior 17(5):367–386. Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |
| [LIT-570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-570.md) | An Organizational Account of Biological Functions | Mossio, Saborido & Moreno (2009), BJPS 60(4):813–841. A trait has a function iff it contributes to the maintenance of a self-maintaining organization, is produced and maintained under that organization's constraints, and the organization is differentiated. Closure grounds teleology and normativity in the current system, unifying etiological and dispositional accounts. Flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes have closure but no functions, because each makes a single undifferentiated contribution to its own maintenance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-444](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-444.md)), from the HAL deposit of the submitted version. Worth reading as the organizational account of function and as the place where the organizational school says plainly that a candle flame has closure. Functions are contributions to a differentiated self-maintaining organization by traits that organization produces and maintains. Closure alone grounds teleology and norms but is shared by flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes; organizational differentiation is what functions need. Reproduction is admitted to be a problem and left to a sketch. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
| [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md) | Conceptualization of the Holobiont Paradigm as It Pertains to Corals | Goulet, Erill, Ascunce, Finley & Javan (2020), Frontiers in Physiology 11:566968, a review. Traits such as thermal tolerance belong to the host–symbiont combination: not every Durusdinium is heat tolerant, and a novel anemone–alga pairing gave higher oxygen flux under heat than both natural ones. Measuring both partners shows different routes to the same bleaching outcome. Whether the holobiont is the unit of selection is asked, not answered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-555.md)); worth reading as a short, explicit statement of why a coral should be studied as a composite of host and microbes rather than as an animal with passengers. The physiological evidence it cites is thin and partly not from corals: its one demonstration that a combination is "not necessarily the sum of its parts" is an oxygen-flux experiment in the sea anemone Exaiptasia. | [LIT-740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-740.md) | Cancer across the tree of life: cooperation and cheating in multicellularity | Aktipis et al. (2015), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 370:20140219. Multicellularity rests on five kinds of cellular cooperation, and cancer is cheating on them. Surveying cancer-like growth across the independent origins of complex multicellularity, the authors find division-of-labour cheating in every form, and resource and environment cheating so far only in animals and plants. Complex multicellularity is a cheater detection and suppression system. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-562](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-562.md)): in full, from the open-access deposit in PubMed Central (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading as a survey of cancer-like growth across the independent origins of multicellularity, read as cheating on five foundations of cooperation: proliferation inhibition, controlled cell death, division of labour, resource allocation and maintenance of the extracellular environment. Cheating on division of labour is reported in every form of multicellularity, and complex multicellularity is described as a cheater detection and suppression system. | [LIT-749](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-749.md) | The Major Transitions in Evolution—A Philosophy-of-Science Perspective | Okasha (2022), Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 10:793824. A major transition is the evolution of a higher-level unit from formerly free-living units. For one to succeed, higher-level selection must trump selection within the collective, typically through policing or aligned interests. The transitions turn the biological hierarchy from explanans into explanandum, vindicate multi-level selection, and leave the highest occupied level privileged as that of organisms. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-586](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-586.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY). Worth reading as a philosopher's map of the major evolutionary transitions. A transition is the evolution of a higher-level unit from formerly free-living ones; for it to succeed, selection between collectives must come to trump selection within them, typically through policing, kinship or division of labour. The transitions make the biological hierarchy something to be explained rather than assumed, and leave the highest occupied level privileged as the level of organisms. Limits: a review with no model or data, provisional by its own account; it cautions that general principles may explain each transition only coarsely. A perspective essay offering a scale-relative, comparative notion of agency. Relative to a chosen decomposition into parts with goals, a whole is agential with respect to its parts when its organization makes them better at resolving their mutual constraints than they would be at the equilibrium of the old organization. This shows as delayed gratification. Citing earlier models, it argues that unsupervised, bottom-up learning among self-interested parts can produce such organization, so that "the agent creates itself". It sets no absolute threshold. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-747](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-747.md)) in full; worth reading as a comparative, scale-relative notion of agency. Given a decomposition into parts with goals of their own, a whole is more agential than its parts when its organization lets them resolve more of their mutual constraints than the old organization did, shown as delayed gratification (going uphill in a specific direction to reach lower minima). Read it knowing that it is a perspective essay. Its model results (Hebbian self-modelling networks, social and ecological networks) are reported from earlier papers. | [LIT-1190](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1190.md) v2 | The physics of symbols: bridging the epistemic cut | Pattee (2001). Evolution requires an epistemic cut between energy-degenerate, rate-independent genetic symbols and the rate-dependent dynamics of construction they control; the same subject–object cut recurs wherever symbols stand for referents, and physics meets it as measurement. The cut is epistemic, not ontological, and arises first at the genotype–phenotype control interface. | Active — read 2026-10-16 in full ([NOTE-952](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-952.md)), from the author-posted text on the Binghamton CASCI site. Read it knowing that it is not measurement-first: the primeval cut is at the genotype–phenotype control interface and "control of construction came first", and measurement presupposes control of the measuring device. The argument rests on von Neumann's regress and Pattee's earlier papers; nothing is derived here. |

| [LIT-1242](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1242.md) v2 | Aggregation of Variables and System Decomposition: Applications to Fitness Landscape Analysis | Shpak, Stadler, Wagner & Hermisson (2004). Separates aggregation of variables, a lower-dimensional map whose dynamics close and which may depend on every microvariable, from decomposition of a system into subsets of variables, and treats systems that are both as a special case, with applications to fitness landscapes. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-979](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-979.md)) in full, from the authors' manuscript in Leipzig University's repository; worth reading for the distinction between aggregation (a closed lower-dimensional description) and decomposition (non-interacting subsets), for the exact condition under which a partition's block sums close in a linear system (column-equitability, [THEORY-755](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-755.md)), and for its application to fitness landscapes, exact for one or two peaks and not for three. Read it knowing that it treats exact aggregation only, paraphrases Simon–Ando without an error bound, states Result 1.1 in a form that fails for some real 2×2 matrices, and overstates in its discussion that every linear aggregation is an equitable partition. |
| [LIT-1356](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1356.md) v2 | What Is Enactivism? | Ward (2026). Treating "enactivism" as an umbrella for any view that stresses sensorimotor loops ignores what sets apart the enactive approach of Varela, Thompson and Rosch: life–mind continuity, the primacy of lived experience, and reciprocity between science and self-understanding. A second axis, organicist against informationalist, runs across the cognitivist–embodied one. Embodied predictive processing, extended functionalism and cybernetics are embodied and informationalist; the enactive approach is organicist. A taxonomy, not an argument that organicism is true. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1065](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1065.md)) from the author's accepted manuscript in the University of Edinburgh repository; worth reading as a short, clear map that separates where a view puts cognition's processes (skull, or brain–body–world) from what it says meaning depends on (information, or organization distinctive of living things). On that map embodied predictive processing, extended functionalism and cybernetics are embodied but informationalist, and the enactive approach of The Embodied Mind is organicist, further marked by the primacy of lived experience and by reciprocity, in which the vocabularies we understand ourselves with reshape the experience they describe. Its main limit is that it argues for a taxonomy, not for organicism, and gives no criterion for which properties are distinctive of life. It does not discuss brains in vats, development or grounding. |
